{{Short description|Function of a matrix}}
{{confuse|Hafnium}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''hafnian''' is a [[Scalar (mathematics)|scalar]] function of a [[symmetric matrix]] that generalizes the [[Permanent (mathematics)|permanent]].

The hafnian was named by [[Eduardo R. Caianiello]] "to mark the fruitful period of stay in [[Copenhagen]] (Hafnia in Latin)."<ref>F. Guerra, in ''Imagination and Rigor: Essays on Eduardo R. Caianiello's Scientific Heritage'', edited by  Settimo Termini, Springer Science & Business Media, 2006, page 98</ref>

== Definition ==

The hafnian of a <math>2n\times 2n</math> symmetric matrix <math>A</math> is defined as
: <math>\operatorname{haf}(A) = \sum_{\rho \in P_{2n}^2} \prod_{\{i,j\} \in \rho} A_{i,j},</math>
where <math>P_{2n}^2</math> is the set of all [[Partition of a set|partitions]] of the set <math>\{1, 2, \dots, 2n\}</math> into subsets of size <math>2</math>.<ref name=":0">{{cite book | title=Combinatorics and Complexity of Partition Functions | page=93 | author=Alexander Barvinok | date=13 March 2017 | publisher=Springer | isbn=9783319518299 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9LlZDgAAQBAJ&pg=PA93}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Weighted counting of integer points in a subspace | journal=Combinator. Probab. Comp. | year=2019 | volume=28 | pages=696–719 | doi=10.1017/S0963548319000105 | arxiv = 1706.05423| last1=Barvinok | first1=Alexander | last2=Regts | first2=Guus | s2cid=126185737 }}</ref>

This definition is similar to that of the [[Pfaffian#Formal definition|Pfaffian]], but differs in that the [[signature (permutation)|signature]]s of the permutations are not taken into account. Thus the relationship of the hafnian to the Pfaffian is the same as relationship of the [[permanent (mathematics)|permanent]] to the [[determinant]].<ref name="Kocharovsky Kocharovsky Tarasov 2022 pp. 144–161">{{cite journal | last1=Kocharovsky | first1=Vitaly V. | last2=Kocharovsky | first2=Vladimir V. | last3=Tarasov | first3=Sergey V. | title=The Hafnian Master Theorem | journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=651 | year=2022 | issn=0024-3795 | doi=10.1016/j.laa.2022.06.021 | pages=144–161| s2cid=249935016 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Basic properties ==

Besides its definition as a sum over perfect pairings, the hafnian of a <math>2n\times 2n</math> symmetric matrix <math>A</math> can equivalently be written as
: <math>\operatorname{haf}(A)=\frac{1}{n!2^n}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{2n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}A_{\sigma(2i-1),\sigma(2i)},</math>
where <math>S_{2n}</math> is the [[symmetric group]] on <math>\{1,2,\dots,2n\}</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=1409.3905 |doi=10.1214/15-AOP1036 |title=Hafnians, perfect matchings and Gaussian matrices |year=2016 |last1=Rudelson |first1=Mark |last2=Samorodnitsky |first2=Alex |last3=Zeitouni |first3=Ofer |journal=The Annals of Probability |volume=44 |issue=4 |pages=2858–2888 |s2cid=14458608 }}</ref>

An equivalent Levi-Civita representation holds for any even-dimensional symmetric matrix <math>V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{N}</math>:
: <math>\operatorname{haf}(V)=\frac{1}{2^{N/2}(N/2)!}\sum_{i_1,\dots,i_N=1}^{N}|\epsilon^{i_1\cdots i_N}|V_{i_1 i_2}\cdots V_{i_{N-1}i_N},</math>
where <math>N</math> is even.<ref name="Ramirez2025">{{cite arXiv |last1=Ramirez Trino |first1=E. A. |last2=Seifi MirJafarlou |first2=M. A. |last3=Rajabpour |first3=M. A. |title=A Generalized Grassmann–Pfaffian Framework for Monomer–Dimer and Spanning Trees |eprint=2511.18495 |class=cond-mat.stat-mech |year=2025}}</ref>

The hafnian also admits a fermionic ([[Berezin integral]]) representation. If <math>V</math> is a symmetric <math>2L\times 2L</math> matrix and <math>\chi_i,\bar{\chi}_i</math> are Grassmann variables, then
: <math>\int D(\chi,\bar{\chi})\,\exp\!\left[\frac{1}{2}(\chi\bar{\chi})^{\mathsf T}V(\chi\bar{\chi})\right]=\operatorname{haf}(V),</math>
where
: <math>(\chi\bar{\chi})^{\mathsf T}=\bigl(\bar{\chi}_1\chi_1,\dots,\bar{\chi}_{2L}\chi_{2L}\bigr)</math>
and
: <math>D(\chi,\bar{\chi})=d\chi_1\,d\bar{\chi}_1\cdots d\chi_{2L}\,d\bar{\chi}_{2L}.</math><ref name="Ramirez2025"/>

For low-dimensional examples,
: <math>\operatorname{haf}\!\begin{pmatrix}V_{11}&V_{12}\\V_{12}&V_{22}\end{pmatrix}=V_{12},</math>
and for a <math>4\times 4</math> symmetric matrix,
: <math>\operatorname{haf}\!\begin{pmatrix}
V_{11}&V_{12}&V_{13}&V_{14}\\
V_{12}&V_{22}&V_{23}&V_{24}\\
V_{13}&V_{23}&V_{33}&V_{34}\\
V_{14}&V_{24}&V_{34}&V_{44}
\end{pmatrix}
=
V_{12}V_{34}+V_{13}V_{24}+V_{14}V_{23}.</math><ref name="Ramirez2025"/>

A useful scaling property is the following. If <math>V=(V_{ij})</math> and <math>S=(S_{ij})</math> are symmetric matrices such that
: <math>V_{ij}=g_i g_j S_{ij},</math>
then, for even <math>N</math>,
: <math>\operatorname{haf}(V)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{N} g_i\right)\operatorname{haf}(S).</math>
In particular, if <math>V=gS</math> for a scalar <math>g</math>, then
: <math>\operatorname{haf}(gS)=g^{N/2}\operatorname{haf}(S).</math><ref name="Ramirez2025"/>

The hafnian of the [[adjacency matrix]] of a graph counts its [[perfect matching]]s (also known as 1-factors). Indeed, a partition of <math>\{1,2,\dots,2n\}</math> into subsets of size 2 is equivalent to a perfect matching of the [[complete graph]] <math>K_{2n}</math>.

The hafnian is closely related to the [[permanent (mathematics)|permanent]]. In particular,
: <math>\operatorname{per}(C)=\operatorname{haf}\begin{pmatrix}
0 & C \\
C^\mathsf{T} & 0
\end{pmatrix}</math>.<ref name=":0" />
Thus, just as the hafnian counts perfect matchings in a graph from its adjacency matrix, the permanent counts matchings in a [[bipartite graph]] from its [[biadjacency matrix]].

The hafnian is also related to moments of [[multivariate Gaussian distribution]]s. By [[Isserlis' theorem|Wick's probability theorem]], for a real <math>2n\times 2n</math> symmetric matrix <math>A</math>,
: <math>\operatorname{haf}(A)=\mathbb E_{\left(X_1,\dots,X_{2n}\right)\sim\mathcal N\left(0,A+\lambda I\right)}\left[X_1\cdots X_{2n}\right],</math>
where <math>\lambda</math> is any number large enough that <math>A+\lambda I</math> is [[positive semi-definite matrix|positive semi-definite]]. Since the hafnian does not depend on the diagonal entries of the matrix, the expectation on the right-hand side is independent of the choice of <math>\lambda</math>.

== Generating function ==

Let <math>S = \begin{pmatrix}
A & C \\
C^\mathsf{T} & B
\end{pmatrix} = S^\mathsf{T}</math> be an arbitrary [[complex number|complex]] symmetric <math>2m \times 2m</math> matrix composed of four <math>m \times m</math> blocks <math>A = A^\mathsf{T}</math>, <math>B = B^\mathsf{T}</math>, <math>C</math> and <math>C^\mathsf{T}</math>. Let <math>z_1, \ldots, z_m</math> be a set of <math>m</math> independent variables, and let <math>Z = 
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & \textrm{diag}(z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_m) \\
\textrm{diag}(z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_m) & 0
\end{pmatrix}</math> be an antidiagonal [[block matrix]] composed of entries <math>z_j</math> (each one is presented twice, one time per nonzero block). Let <math>I</math> denote the [[identity matrix]]. Then the following identity holds:<ref name="Kocharovsky Kocharovsky Tarasov 2022 pp. 144–161" />
: <math>
\frac{1}{\sqrt{\det \big(I - Z S\big) }} = \sum_{\{n_k\}} \operatorname{haf} \tilde{S}(\{n_k\}) \prod_{k=1}^m \frac{z_k^{n_k}}{n_k!}
</math>
where the right-hand side involves hafnians of <math>\Big(2\sum_k n_k\Big)\times\Big(2\sum_k n_k\Big)</math> matrices <math>\tilde{S}(\{n_k\}) = \begin{pmatrix}
\tilde{A}(\{n_k\}) & \tilde{C}(\{n_k\}) \\
\tilde{C}^\mathsf{T}(\{n_k\}) & \tilde{B}(\{n_k\}) \\
\end{pmatrix}</math>, whose blocks <math>\tilde{A}(\{n_k\})</math>, <math>\tilde{B}(\{n_k\})</math>, <math>\tilde{C}(\{n_k\})</math> and <math>\tilde{C}^\mathsf{T}(\{n_k\})</math> are built from the blocks <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C
</math> and <math>C^\mathsf{T}</math> respectively in the way introduced in [[MacMahon's master theorem|MacMahon's Master theorem]]. In particular, <math>\tilde{A}(\{n_k\})</math> is a matrix built by replacing each entry <math>A_{k,t}</math> in the matrix <math>A</math> with a <math>n_k \times n_t</math> block filled with <math>A_{k,t}</math>; the same scheme is applied to <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> and <math>C^\mathsf{T}</math>. The sum <math>\sum_{\{n_k\}}</math> runs over all <math>k</math>-tuples of non-negative [[integer]]s, and it is assumed that <math>\operatorname{haf} \tilde{S}(\{n_k=0|k=1\ldots m\}) = 1</math>.

The identity can be [[mathematical proof|proved]]<ref name="Kocharovsky Kocharovsky Tarasov 2022 pp. 144–161" /> by means of multivariate [[Gaussian integral]]s and [[Isserlis' theorem|Wick's probability theorem]].

The expression in the left-hand side, <math>1 \Big/ \sqrt{\det \big(I - Z S\big)} \Big. </math>, is in fact a multivariate [[generating function]] for a series of hafnians, and the right-hand side constitutes its multivariable [[Taylor expansion]] in the vicinity of the point  <math>z_1 = \ldots = z_m = 0.</math>  As a consequence of the given relation, the hafnian of a symmetric <math>2m \times 2m</math> matrix <math>S</math> can be represented as the following mixed [[derivative]] of the order <math>m</math>:
: <math>
\operatorname{haf}S = \bigg(\prod_{k=1}^m \frac{\partial}{\partial z_k} \bigg) \Bigg.\frac{1}{\sqrt{\det \big(I - Z S\big)}} \Bigg\vert_{z_j=0}.
</math>

The hafnian generating function identity written above can be considered as a hafnian generalization of [[MacMahon's master theorem|MacMahon's Master theorem]], which introduces the generating function for [[Matrix permanent|matrix permanents]] and has the following form in terms of the introduced notation:

:<math>
\frac{1}{\det \big(I - \textrm{diag} (z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_m) C\big)} = \sum_{\{n_k\}} \operatorname{per} \tilde{C}(\{n_k\}) \prod_{k=1}^m \frac{z_k^{n_k}}{n_k!}   
</math>

Note that MacMahon's Master theorem comes as a simple [[corollary]] from the hafnian generating function identity due to the relation <math>\operatorname{per} (C) = \operatorname{haf} \begin{pmatrix}
0 & C \\
C^\mathsf{T} & 0
\end{pmatrix}</math>.

== Non-negativity ==

If <math>C</math> is a Hermitian [[Positive semi-definite matrix|positive semi-definite]] <math>n\times n</math> matrix and <math>B</math> is a complex symmetric <math>n\times n</math> matrix, then
: <math>\operatorname{haf}\begin{pmatrix}
B & C \\
\overline{C} & \overline{B}
\end{pmatrix}\geq 0,</math>
where <math>\overline{C}</math> denotes the [[complex conjugate]] of <math>C</math>.<ref name="Brádler Friedland Israel 2021 pp. 4615–4619">{{cite journal | last1=Brádler | first1=Kamil | last2=Friedland | first2=Shmuel | last3=Israel | first3=Robert B. | title=Nonnegativity for hafnians of certain matrices | journal=Linear and Multilinear Algebra | publisher=Informa UK Limited | volume=70 | issue=19 | date=2021-02-24 | issn=0308-1087 | doi=10.1080/03081087.2021.1892022 | pages=4615–4619| arxiv=1811.10342 | s2cid=119601142 }}</ref>

A simple way to see this when <math>\begin{pmatrix}
C & B \\
\overline{B} & \overline{C} \\
\end{pmatrix}</math> is positive semi-definite is to observe that, by [[Isserlis' theorem|Wick's probability theorem]], <math>\operatorname{haf}\begin{pmatrix}
B & C \\
\overline{C} & \overline{B} \\
\end{pmatrix}=\mathbb E\left[\left|X_1\dots X_n\right|^2\right]</math> when <math>\left(X_1,\dots,X_n\right)</math> is a [[complex normal distribution|complex normal random vector]] with mean <math>0</math>, [[covariance matrix]] <math>C</math> and relation matrix <math>B</math>.

This result is a generalization of the fact that the permanent of a Hermitian positive semi-definite matrix is non-negative. This corresponds to the special case <math>B=0</math> using the relation <math>\operatorname{per} (C) = \operatorname{haf} \begin{pmatrix}
0 & C \\
C^\mathsf{T} & 0
\end{pmatrix}</math>.

== Loop hafnian ==

The loop hafnian of an <math>m\times m</math> symmetric matrix is defined as
: <math>\operatorname{lhaf}(A) = \sum_{\rho \in \mathcal{M}} \prod_{(i,j) \in \rho} A_{i,j}</math>
where <math>\mathcal{M}</math> is the set of all perfect matchings of the complete graph on <math>m</math> vertices ''with [[loop (graph theory)|loop]]s'', i.e., the set of all ways to partition the set <math>\{1, 2, \dots, m\}</math> into pairs or singletons (treating a singleton <math>(i)</math> as the pair <math>(i, i)</math>).<ref name="Björklund Gupt Quesada p. "/> Thus the loop hafnian depends on the diagonal entries of the matrix, unlike the hafnian.<ref name="Björklund Gupt Quesada p. "/> Furthermore, the loop hafnian can be non-zero when <math>m</math> is odd.

The loop hafnian can be used to count the total number of matchings in a graph (perfect or non-perfect), also known as its [[Hosoya index]]. Specifically, if one takes the [[adjacency matrix]] of a graph and sets the diagonal elements to 1, then the loop hafnian of the resulting matrix is equal to the total number of matchings in the graph.<ref name="Björklund Gupt Quesada p. ">{{cite arXiv | last1=Björklund | first1=Andreas | last2=Gupt | first2=Brajesh | last3=Quesada | first3=Nicolás | title=A faster hafnian formula for complex matrices and its benchmarking on a supercomputer | year=2018 | eprint=1805.12498 | page=| class=cs.DS }}</ref>

The loop hafnian can also be thought of as incorporating a mean into the interpretation of the hafnian as a multivariate Gaussian moment. Specifically, by [[Isserlis' theorem|Wick's probability theorem]] again, the loop hafnian of a real <math>m\times m</math> symmetric matrix can be expressed as
: <math>
\operatorname{lhaf}(A) = \mathbb E_{\left(X_1,\dots,X_m\right)\sim\mathcal N\left(\operatorname{diag}\left(A\right),A+\lambda I\right)}\left[X_1\dots X_m\right],
</math>
where <math>\lambda</math> is any number large enough to make <math>A+\lambda I</math> positive semi-definite.

== Computation ==

Computing the hafnian of a (0,1)-matrix is [[sharp-P-complete|#P-complete]], because [[♯P-completeness_of_01-permanent|computing the permanent of a (0,1)-matrix is #P-complete]].<ref name="Kocharovsky Kocharovsky Tarasov 2022 pp. 144–161" /><ref name="Björklund Gupt Quesada p. "/>

The hafnian of a <math>2n\times 2n</math> matrix can be computed in <math>O(n^3 2^n)</math> time.<ref name="Björklund Gupt Quesada p. "/>

If the entries of a matrix are non-negative, then its hafnian can be approximated to within an exponential factor in polynomial time.<ref name="Barvinok 1999 pp. 29–61">{{cite journal | last=Barvinok | first=Alexander | title=Polynomial Time Algorithms to Approximate Permanents and Mixed Discriminants Within a Simply Exponential Factor | journal=Random Structures and Algorithms | publisher=Wiley | volume=14 | issue=1 | year=1999 | issn=1042-9832 | doi=10.1002/(sici)1098-2418(1999010)14:1<29::aid-rsa2>3.0.co;2-x | pages=29–61| hdl=2027.42/35110 | hdl-access=free }}</ref>
